etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English riches, plural of riche (“power, wealth”), from Old English rīċe (“power, authority, dominion”). Confused with Middle English richesse (“wealth”), from Old French richesse, from riche (“rich, wealthy”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *rīki (“rich”) from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“rich, powerful”), from Proto-Indo-European *reg- (“to straighten, direct, make right”). Akin to Old High German rīhhi (“rich”) (German reich (“rich”)), Old English rīċe (“rich”), Old English racu (“explanation, reasoning”). More at rich.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii], page 12:
quote.text: Cal. […] Sometimes a thouſand twangling Inſtruments  Will hum about mine eares ; and ſometime voices,  That if I then had wak'd after long ſleepe,  Will make me ſleepe againe, and then in dreaming,  The clouds methought would open, and ſhew riches  Ready to drop vpon me, that when I wak'd  I cri'de to dreame againe.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From rich +‎ -es (plural suffix) by analogy with poors (“poor people”).

quote.text: Mr. Chander Lall Mookerji wrote to me thus: “The youngs and the olds, the highs and the lows, the riches and the poors, all join together in praising Your Honour’s magnanimity.”
